title: NASA Spins Mars Helicopter Blades Faster Than Sound
summary:
Flying a helicopter on Mars is one of the hardest tricks in space exploration. The air there is only about 1% as thick as Earth's air, so the blades have almost nothing to push against. To get enough lift, they have to spin incredibly fast — so fast that their tips can break the sound barrier.

NASA engineers have now tested just how fast new Mars helicopter blades can go. In March, at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, they spun experimental blades inside a giant chamber filled with carbon dioxide to copy the thin Martian air. Across 137 test runs, the blades held together even as their tips raced past the speed of sound.

The first rotor had three blades. It reached 3,750 spins per minute, with its tips at Mach 0.98, just below the speed of sound. Then engineers switched on a fan to blow headwinds at the spinning blades, pushing the tips faster still. A second rotor, built for NASA's SkyFall project, had two slightly longer blades and reached the same near-supersonic speed at 3,570 spins per minute.

On the final runs, the blade tips hit Mach 1.08 — faster than sound. 'We thought we'd be lucky to hit Mach 1.05, and we reached Mach 1.08 on our last runs,' said Shannah Withrow-Maser, an aerodynamicist at NASA's Ames Research Center.

That extra power matters. NASA's first Mars helicopter, Ingenuity, made history on April 19, 2021, as the first aircraft to fly on another world, but it was built mainly to prove flight was possible. Its blades were limited to 2,700 spins per minute to stay safely away from the sound barrier. Future helicopters could carry heavier science instruments, bigger batteries, and advanced sensors, flying low over Mars to scout for robotic and human missions.
why_it_matters: Faster, stronger blades could let future Mars helicopters carry heavier science tools and scout ahead for robotic and human missions, helping us explore another world more safely.

keywords.explanation: Lift is the upward push that raises an aircraft into the air.
The sound barrier is the point where something moves as fast as sound.
Carbon dioxide is a gas that filled the test chamber to copy the thin air on Mars.
A rotor is the spinning part of a helicopter that holds its blades.
Mach is a way to measure speed by comparing it with the speed of sound.
An aerodynamicist is a scientist who studies how air moves around things that fly.

background_read: A helicopter flies because its spinning blades push against the air, and that push lifts it up.
On Mars the air is far thinner than on Earth, so blades have almost nothing to push against and must spin much faster to get enough lift.
That is why NASA tests new blades in a chamber filled with carbon dioxide, which copies the thin air on Mars, before trusting them on a real flight.
The first Mars helicopter, Ingenuity, showed that flight on another world was possible, and faster blades could let future helicopters carry heavier science gear.
